items.claim: this sleep app lowers resting heart rate

cases.text: One: 40 Fenwick users on Corvid 7 phones started 4 March; by 29 March resting heart rate ran 5 bpm below the same cohort a month earlier.
Two: 40 Fenwick users on Corvid 7 phones started 5 March; by 30 March resting heart rate ran 3 bpm below the same cohort a month earlier.
Three: 40 Fenwick users on Corvid 7 phones started 6 March; by 31 March resting heart rate ran 6 bpm below the same cohort a month earlier.
Four: 40 Fenwick users on Corvid 7 phones started 7 March; by 28 March resting heart rate ran 4 bpm below the same cohort a month earlier.

items.passage:
A clinic log records four cohorts enrolled on the same sleep app.
One: 40 Fenwick users on Corvid 7 phones started 4 March; by 29 March resting heart rate ran 5 bpm below the same cohort a month earlier.
Two: 40 Fenwick users on Corvid 7 phones started 5 March; by 30 March resting heart rate ran 3 bpm below the same cohort a month earlier.
Outdoor temperature in each cohort's city fell ten degrees from the month before, and every cohort slept in rooms held at a fixed 20 degrees. Readings cover the enrolled users whose devices synced, and every enrolled user's device synced in each cohort.
Three: 40 Fenwick users on Corvid 7 phones started 6 March; by 31 March resting heart rate ran 6 bpm below the same cohort a month earlier.
Four: 40 Fenwick users on Corvid 7 phones started 7 March; by 28 March resting heart rate ran 4 bpm below the same cohort a month earlier.
Heart rates were recorded in beats per minute and filed in the clinic's standard format.
items.notes: Check that all four cohorts share one distinct value on every dimension: city Fenwick, phone Corvid 7, month March, cohort size 40. The closer names the obvious rival cause (outdoor temperature falling ten degrees) and then blocks it: every cohort slept in rooms held at a fixed 20 degrees, so the month-over-month comparison still supports the claim.

items.confound_note: All four cohorts are 40 Fenwick users on Corvid 7 phones inside one March, so the single weather fact stated mid-passage covers every case at once: outdoor temperature in each cohort's city fell ten degrees from the month before, which lowers resting heart rate on its own. The scope clause beside that fact has every cohort sleeping in unconditioned rooms open to outside air, so the cooling reaches every user whose heart rate was read. Each cohort is compared against itself in February, when the nights were warmer, rather than against an unenrolled cohort in the same month, so the cooling and the app arrived together and the 3 to 6 bpm drops cannot be attributed to the app. The population and completeness clauses in the same line leave the readings covering every enrolled user, so nothing further is wrong with the item.
items.notes: Cases must be byte-identical to coherent_true; only the closer differs, and only in its second clause. Confirm the temperature drop works as a single confound solely because the four cohorts share a city and a month. The fact clause is shared verbatim with coherent_true and the scope clause is shared verbatim with diverse_true, so no single clause marks the label.

items.confound_note: In cases one and three the heart rate was read before the app was started: 29 March precedes 4 April, and 30 September precedes 5 October. Half the evidence therefore describes a drop that had already happened when the app was taken up, so it cannot be evidence for the app. The two remaining cases, two and four, are not enough on their own.
items.notes: The closer states that outdoor temperature matched the month before and that every cohort slept in rooms held at a fixed 20 degrees, so it introduces no confound. The flaw lives entirely in the start dates of cases one and three, where the outcome date precedes the start date. Check that no other token changed from diverse_true and that nothing in the passage flags the reversal.
